extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for International Searching Authorities on which subject-matter is excluded from international search and preliminary examination under the PCT, and how to determine the extent of search when applications have excluded subject-matter or compliance defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific and Mathematical Theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of scientific or mathematical theories in claims does not immediately exclude the claims from search or preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When viewing the claims as a whole, if the theories are applied or implemented to produce a practical application or to have technical character, search and preliminary examination is required since the result is not purely abstract or intellectual. Examples: the physical theory of semi-conductivity would be excluded, whereas new semiconductor devices and processes for manufacturing would require search; a shortcut method of division is excluded but a calculating machine designed to operate accordingly would require search and preliminary examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant or Animal Varieties and Essentially Biological Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant and animal varieties may be excluded from search, but transgenic plants, genetically modified non-human animals, and methods of making these types of inventions would be searched and examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a process is 'essentially biological' is one of degree and depends on the extent of technical intervention by man; simple selective breeding is essentially biological (excluded), while application of growth-stimulating substances, radiation treatments, cloning or genetic manipulation are not essentially biological and are to be searched. Microbiological processes and their products are not excluded; 'product of a microbiological process' (including plasmids and viruses) may be searched and can be protected per se. Propagation of a product of a microbiological process is treated as a microbiological process for Rules 39 and 67.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes, Rules or Methods of Doing Business, Mental Acts, or Playing Games
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes, rules or methods of doing business, performing purely mental acts or playing games are examples of items of an abstract or intellectual character and may be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination focuses on whether the claimed invention is of an abstract character rather than on the art or classification. Where divergent practices exist between Authorities, specific guidance is set out in the appendix to the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of Treatment by Surgery or Therapy; Diagnostic Methods Practiced on the Human or Animal Body
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy, and diagnostic methods practiced on the human or animal body, are subject-matter on which an Authority is not required to carry out international search or preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruments, apparatus, and new products (e.g., substances or compositions) for use in such methods should be searched and examined. The exclusion applies only to methods actually limited to being carried out on a living human or animal body; treatments on dead bodies or on removed tissues/fluids (not returned to the same body) are not excluded (e.g., blood bank storage or diagnostic testing). Prophylactic methods (immunization) are considered therapeutic and may be excluded. Cosmetic treatment by administration of a chemical product should be searched; cosmetic surgery may be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Presentations of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Any presentation of information characterized solely by the content of the information is excluded under Rules 39 and 67.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers presentation per se (acoustical signals, spoken words, visual displays), information recorded on carriers (books, records, magnetic tapes characterized solely by content), and processes/apparatus for presenting information characterized solely by the information indicated or recorded. If the presentation of encoded information has technical character or both a structural and functional relationship to the information carrier, process or apparatus, these should be examined. Examples: a measuring device with volumetric markings interacting with a receptacle (recalibration), a gramophone record with a particular groove form to allow stereo, or a diapositive with a sound track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Arrangements or Compilations of Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere arrangements or compilations of data are generally excluded subject-matter unless the arrangement or manner of presentation has technical character or a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere program listing that is not capable of execution represents mere expression of the underlying idea and is excluded. A disembodied data structure with no interaction with an underlying program does not require international search/examination. A data structure embodied in a tangible medium that has technical character or a practical application should be subject to search and examination. Examples in bioinformatics illustrate excluded and non-excluded cases (see Examples 1 and 2): 3-D structural data of a protein per se (excluded); an in silico screening method applying a molecular modeling algorithm (has technical character and is searched), while a database encoded merely with identified compounds (disembodied data) may be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer Programs (to the Extent Authority is not Equipped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs are excluded subject-matter to the extent that the Authority is not equipped to carry out search or preliminary examination on such programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normally, claims that merely recite program code are excluded. However, if a natural language description of a computer-executable program or self-documented code is included in the description and claims, the Authority may be considered equipped to carry out a search and preliminary examination based on such a description, subject to other exclusion conditions. Authorities have diverging practices; see appendix for guidance where practices differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of Claims — focus on content not form
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering whether excluded subject-matter under Rule 39 or 67 is present, the examiner disregards the form or kind of claim and concentrates on the content to identify the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion applies only to the extent the application relates to excluded subject matter. Example: a gramophone record distinguished solely by music recorded would be excluded, but if the groove form is modified so the record functions in a new way (technical feature), the claimed subject-matter could undergo search and preliminary examination. Examiner should not apply criteria more restrictively than for national applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded Matter in Only Some Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where only some claims comprise excluded subject-matter, this is indicated in the international search report, written opinion and the international preliminary examination report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search and preliminary examination are conducted for the other claims that are not excluded. Reports should identify which claims were excluded from search/preliminary examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases of Doubt — perform search to the extent possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of doubt as to whether claimed subject-matter constitutes excluded subject-matter, the Authority carries out the search or preliminary examination to the extent possible using the available documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doubt exists, proceed with whatever meaningful search/examination can be done; record limitations in reports/opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Search When Application Fails to Comply with Prescribed Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If description, claims or drawings fail to comply to such an extent that a meaningful search cannot be carried out for a particular claim, no search may be possible; if parts can be sufficiently understood, a search is performed taking non-compliance into account in determining extent of search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The international search report and written opinion should indicate how the application fails to comply and specify to what degree that non-compliance has been taken into account in determining the extent of the search (as precisely as possible). In general, a search should be carried out to the maximum extent practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Search Is Possible Despite Defects — indicate non-prior-art objections and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a search can be carried out despite defects (e.g., lack of support, claims defined solely by result, unusual parameters, Markush claims, multitudinous claims), the written opinion should include observations on non-prior-art grounds (sufficiency, support, clarity, conciseness) and explain extent of search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate search strategy: search first for embodiments disclosed in description, then extend to broader relevant areas but need not search areas of low probability. Written opinion should identify non-prior-art objections (e.g., lack of support, lack of clarity, inability to determine parameters), and specify which parts were searched (e.g., disclosed examples, structural generalizations). For Markush-type or unclear/multitudinous claims, search may be limited to clearly disclosed or clearly prepared/tested embodiments and structural generalizations thereof; indicate precisely how objections were taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: When No Search at All Is Possible — declaration under Article 17(2)(a)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: When none of the claims can be meaningfully searched at all because no likely amendment can be determined to overcome the non-compliance, the International Searching Authority makes a declaration under Article 17(2)(a)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only some claims cannot be meaningfully searched, indicate this in the international search report under Article 17(2)(b) and search other claims as usual. Written opinion should object on non-prior-art grounds (Article 6/Rule 6 etc.) and indicate to what degree the objection has been taken into account when determining that no search at all is possible. Examples: nonsensical or purely aspirational claims ('My invention is worth a million dollars'), undefined fictitious materials ('kryptonite'), or multitudinous overlapping claims with no reasonable basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Prior-Art Issues to be Considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Searches regarding non-prior-art issues include clarity of claims, conciseness and number of claims, support in the description, clear and complete disclosure, sufficiency commensurate with the claims, relationship of claims to disclosure, and new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed guidance and discussion of these non-prior-art concerns are contained in Chapter 5 (paragraphs 5.31 to 5.58) and paragraphs referenced for new matter (20.20, 20.21). If industrial applicability opinion is negative, cite prior art used and set out reasoning in the written opinion; indicate any implications for novelty/inventive step where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal Clarification from Applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: If defects prevent a meaningful search, the International Searching Authority may, where appropriate, ask the applicant informally for clarification before declaring that no international search report will be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner may also ask for clarification when no opinion is possible on novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability for all or part of the claimed subject-matter. Such informal clarification is not an invitation to file amendments. Even after clarification, the examiner must still make objections on non-prior-art grounds where appropriate and explain remaining deficiencies in the written opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclear Claims — search clear realizations; determine reasonable expected subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed subject-matter includes alternatives, some clear and some unclear, the search examiner searches the clear realization(s) and determines the subject of search for unclear realizations based on what might reasonably be expected to be claimed by amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner takes into account description, drawings and common general knowledge to identify reasonable claimable subject-matter and conducts the search accordingly. If an alternative is totally unclear such that subject-matter cannot be determined, that alternative need not be searched. Examples provided with combinations of alternatives illustrate which combinations to search and which may be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual Motion Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application pertaining to perpetual motion is not necessarily excluded from searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The International Searching Authority should endeavor to search such an application unless it is so unclear that Article 17(2)(a) requires a declaration of no search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence Listings — requirements and limited searching
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application contains nucleotide and/or amino acid sequence disclosures required in a sequence listing but the Authority does not have an acceptable sequence listing complying with standards and in an accepted language, the Authority requests provision of such a listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the listing is not provided in the required form or language, the Authority makes a meaningful search or preliminary examination to the extent possible (e.g., search by a named protein rather than sequence). Note sequences with fewer than ten specifically defined nucleotides or fewer than four specifically defined amino acids are not required to be included in a sequence listing.
